justification_text:
My point estimates were anchored primarily to the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, with a modest upward drift built in at each horizon. The 1-day estimate of 1053 reflects near-term momentum and mean-reversion tendencies, assuming no major overnight shock. The 1-week estimate of 1058 incorporates a slight positive drift consistent with longer-term trend behavior, while the 1-month estimate of 1065 extends that drift further but remains relatively conservative, acknowledging that sustained directional moves are difficult to predict and that mean-reversion forces tend to dampen extreme outcomes over medium horizons.

The confidence interval widths reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At the 1-day horizon, the 46-point range is relatively tight, driven primarily by typical daily volatility. By one week, the interval widens to roughly 96 points, incorporating the possibility of multi-day trending moves or reversals that can accumulate. At one month, the 190-point range reflects the full scope of plausible outcomes when compounding daily volatility over approximately 20 trading sessions, along with the possibility of regime shifts in sentiment or macroeconomic conditions. The widths were calibrated using a rough volatility-scaling approach, where uncertainty grows approximately with the square root of time.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in risk sentiment — such as an unexpected central bank policy shift, geopolitical escalation, or a financial contagion event — could drive prices well below the lower bounds, particularly at the 1-month horizon. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected macroeconomic data release, a coordinated policy stimulus, or a short-squeeze dynamic could push prices above the upper bounds. Liquidity conditions also matter: in thin markets, price moves can overshoot fundamentally justified levels before correcting.

It is also worth noting that these intervals represent 90% confidence bounds, meaning there is an inherent 10% probability assigned to outcomes outside the stated range. Fat-tailed distributions in financial markets mean that truly extreme moves — several standard deviations from the point estimate — occur more frequently than a normal distribution would suggest. Black swan events, by definition, are not well-captured by historical volatility-based calibration, so the true tail risk is likely somewhat larger than what the intervals formally imply.
